title: Longest Subsequence With Steady Pair Remainders
statement:
You get an array of positive integers nums and a number k. A subsequence (elements kept in their original order, gaps allowed) is steady if every two neighbors in it have a sum with the same remainder modulo k:

(s[0] + s[1]) mod k = (s[1] + s[2]) mod k = … = (s[m−2] + s[m−1]) mod k

Return the length of the longest steady subsequence. Any two elements form a steady subsequence, so the answer is at least 2.

examples.why: Take 1, 4, 1, 4. Each leaves remainder 1, so every neighbor sum leaves remainder 2.
Take 3, 5, 9, 2, 6 with remainders 0, 2, 0, 2, 0. Every neighbor sum leaves remainder 2. The values need not be equal; their remainders alternate.
Two elements are always steady: there is only one neighbor sum.

hints: Write out (a + b) ≡ (b + c) mod k. What does it say about a and c?
It says a ≡ c. So in a steady subsequence the remainders alternate between two values x, y (possibly equal). Only remainders matter, not the numbers.

Let best[r][p] be the longest steady subsequence ending with remainder r whose previous element has remainder p. A new element with remainder r extends best[p][r] for every p: best[r][p] = best[p][r] + 1.

explain.intuition:
From (a + b) ≡ (b + c) you can cancel b and get a ≡ c (mod k). So in a steady subsequence every element has the same remainder as the one two places before it: the remainders go x, y, x, y, …. That turns the problem into "longest subsequence whose remainders alternate between some pair x, y".

Track best[r][p] = longest such subsequence that ends in remainder r right after remainder p. When a number with remainder r arrives, it can follow any subsequence ending in p whose previous remainder was r, so best[r][p] = best[p][r] + 1 for every p. A best[p][r] of 0 means "no element yet", and the formula then sets 1, a subsequence of just this element waiting for a partner. That is k updates per element, O(n · k) overall.
steps: Make a k × k table best filled with 0.
For each number, let r = x mod k.
For every p from 0 to k − 1, set best[r][p] = best[p][r] + 1 and update the answer.
pitfalls: Fixing the pair-sum remainder from the first two picked elements and greedily extending. Choosing a different pair later can give a longer chain.
Thinking the values must repeat. Only remainders matter, so 3, 5, 9, 2, 6 works for k = 3.
Trying every target remainder with its own O(n²) pass. It is correct, but at n = k = 1000 that is about a billion steps.

solutions.title: Fix the target sum, then LIS-style DP
solutions.idea: For each target remainder s, f[i] = longest steady subsequence ending at i whose neighbor sums are s, built from every earlier j.

solutions.title: DP over pairs of positions
solutions.idea: dp[i][s] = longest steady subsequence ending at i with neighbor-sum remainder s; extend from every earlier j with s = (nums[j] + nums[i]) mod k.

solutions.title: Remainder-pair table
solutions.idea: Remainders alternate x, y, x, y. best[r][p] is the longest chain ending in remainder r after remainder p; a new r extends best[p][r].

followups: k = 2 only. Can you solve it with a handful of counters instead of a table?
